tips: Standard cold-pressed lemon and sweet orange essential oils fade quickly in cold process soap. For a citrus scent that survives cure, use folded citrus oils (5x or 10x lemon or orange) and/or anchor the blend with litsea cubeba (may chang) or lemongrass, which keep their sparkling lemony scent long-term.

Most citrus essential oils (lemon, orange, lime, bergamot, litsea cubeba) have a conservative maximum usage rate of about 3% of the recipe by weight, which works out to roughly 0.48 oz (13.6 g, about 3 tsp) per pound (454 g) of soaping oils.

Phototoxicity from furanocoumarins in cold-pressed bergamot, lime, and other expressed citrus oils applies to leave-on products in sunlight; in a wash-off product like bar soap the risk is negligible. Bergaptene-free (FCF) bergamot and distilled lemon or lime are non-phototoxic options if you want zero concern.

The natural sugars in citrus juice can scorch and overheat cold process soap, causing discoloration, heat tunnels, or even a soap volcano. Chill or freeze juice before combining it with lye and soap cool, around 100-110F. Finely ground dried zest is the safer choice: it adds golden speckles and light exfoliation rather than scent.
Calendula petals are the classic topping and mix-in for citrus bars because they keep their golden yellow-orange color in cold process soap, while most other flower petals fade or turn brown.
